pr_summary: Add existence-of-base machinery for crystallographic root systems: define indecomposable "baseOf" and prove generation/closure lemmas; add lemmas linking pairing/coefficient maps and prove linear independence of the base-of-roots (over ℚ and over the ground field) using a positive form.

declarations.name: Algebra.Group.Hom.invMonoidHom_comp_invMonoidHom
declarations.nl_statement: Composition of the inversion monoid homomorphism with itself is the identity monoid homomorphism.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: This is a one-line check: extensionality on elements and simplification using inv_inv = id; the proof uses `ext` and `simp` to verify the equality of functions.

declarations.name: IsMulIndecomposable.baseOf
declarations.nl_statement: Definition: given a family v : ι → M and a monoid hom f : M →* S, define baseOf v f as the subset of indices i with 1 < f (v i) which are indecomposable relative to that subset.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: This is a straightforward definition wrapping the existing IsMulIndecomposable predicate with the half-space {i | 1 < f (v i)}. No proof, just a definition; subsequent lemmas refer to it.

declarations.name: IsMulIndecomposable.image_baseOf_inv_comp_eq
declarations.nl_statement: For an involutive index inversion, a commutative group v : ι → G with known inverses, and ordered monoid S, the image of baseOf under v after precomposing f with inversion equals the image of baseOf under the inverted v and original f.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The proof reduces to showing one inclusion, then uses symmetry via composing with invMonoidHom and the fact that invMonoidHom ∘ invMonoidHom = id. Concretely the lemma converts a membership statement about i to one about i⁻¹ and rewrites equalities using the hypothesis v i⁻¹ = (v i)⁻¹, then applies the indecomposability condition; the final step is handled by `aesop`.

declarations.name: Submonoid.closure_image_isMulIndecomposable_baseOf
declarations.nl_statement: For finite index set ι and linearly ordered target S, the submonoid generated by the v-images of indecomposable indices in the half-space equals the submonoid generated by all v-images in that half-space. I.e., indecomposable elements generate the same closure as the whole half-space.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The proof follows Serre's lemma: prove closure of the image of the indecomposable subset equals closure of the image of {i | 1 < f (v i)}. One direction is immediate by monotonicity. For the other, assume some v i in the half-space is not in the closure of the indecomposables, build the set s of indices in the half-space whose images are not yet generated, pick a minimal element with respect to f ◦ v (using finiteness), and show it decomposes as a product of two strictly smaller elements (by f-value), so each factor lies in the closure by minimality, contradicting the non-membership. The Lean proof encodes this minimality argument with finite minimal-for and manipulates closure membership via `closure`/`mul_mem` etc; `aesop` and small rewrites are used where appropriate.

declarations.name: Subgroup.closure_image_isMulIndecomposable_baseOf
declarations.nl_statement: Under the group/involution hypotheses and that no image under f equals 1, the subgroup generated by the indecomposable baseOf equals the subgroup generated by the whole range of v (i.e., indecomposables generate the whole group).
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: This uses the Submonoid version for the positive half-space and then applies the same argument to the inverse half-space by composing f with inversion. The proof rewrites the universe as union of the two half-spaces (since no value equals 1), applies the submonoid closure lemma to the positive half-space and to the inverted one via `invMonoidHom`, and then uses image/inversion identities and closure_inv to assemble the equality for the subgroup closure. The argument in Lean is a straightforward translation of this inversion trick, with small bookkeeping using `image_comp` and `image_inv_eq_inv`.

declarations.name: IsMulIndecomposable.pairwise_div_notMem_range
declarations.nl_statement: Given a family v : ι → G (G commutative group) with no element equal to 1, an involution on indices, a set s of indecomposable indices relative to t, and the hypothesis every index or its inverse lies in t, the pairwise ratios v i / v j for i≠j from s are not in the range of v.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: A combinatorial exclusion: assume v i / v j = v k for some k, and use the fact k or k⁻¹ lies in t together with indecomposability of i or j to derive a contradiction. Proof in Lean pattern-matches on which side k or k⁻¹ belongs to t and builds the forbidden decomposition, finishing by `simp` and logical manipulations. Straightforward and mirrors the math argument directly.

declarations.name: IsMulIndecomposable.pairwise_div_notMem_range'
declarations.nl_statement: Variant: under the ordered-monoid valuation f, if s is included in the baseOf set, then the same pairwise non-membership of ratios holds.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: This reduces to the previous lemma by observing that the hypothesis f(v i) ≠ 1 prevents v i = 1 and that every index or its inverse is in the half-space {i | 1 < f(v i)} (up to value comparisons). The Lean proof constructs the nontrivial `hv_one` and supplies the required membership alternative, then applies the previous lemma.

declarations.name: IsMulIndecomposable.pairwise_baseOf_div_notMem
declarations.nl_statement: Specialization: the elements of baseOf v f are pairwise such that their ratios are not in the range of v.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Direct one-line specialization of pairwise_div_notMem_range' taking s = baseOf v f and reflexivity of inclusion. The Lean lemma is a trivial wrapper.

declarations.name: IsMulIndecomposable.mem_or_inv_mem_closure_baseOf
declarations.nl_statement: For finite index ι and group hypotheses, every v i or its inverse belongs to the submonoid closure generated by v '' baseOf v f.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: This follows from Subgroup.closure_image_isMulIndecomposable_baseOf (which equates closures) and splitting the possible sign of f(v i) (less or greater than 1) using the hypothesis f(v i) ≠ 1; one of i or i⁻¹ then lies in the positive half-space and hence its image lies in the closure. The Lean proof is a concise case split and application of closure lemmas and subset_closure.

declarations.name: RootPairing.baseOf_pairwise_pairing_le_zero
declarations.nl_statement: (Serre V.§9 Lemma 3) For a crystallographic RootPairing P and an additive valuation f with f(root) nonzero, the indices in baseOf P.root f have non-positive integer pairings: for distinct i,j in the base, pairingIn ℤ i j ≤ 0.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The proof reduces to the additive indecomposable variant: apply IsAddIndecomposable.pairwise_baseOf_sub_notMem on the root family (translation of multiplicative statements to additive ones) to get that no positive pairing can occur; contraposing yields the desired non-positivity via P.root_sub_root_mem_of_pairingIn_pos which converts a positive integer pairing into a decomposition contradicting indecomposability. The Lean proof is terse but follows the exact math steps, using the `indexNeg` instance to handle sign conventions and `aesop` in the supporting lemma.

declarations.name: RootPairing.linearIndepOn_root_baseOf'
declarations.nl_statement: Given a RootPairing P over R valued in S (S an ordered commutative ring embedded in R) and a dual functional f with nonzero values on roots, the roots indexed by baseOf (with respect to f) are linearly independent over S in the S-span of the roots.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: This is the key linear-algebra step: restrict attention to M₀ = span_S(range roots) and consider the list v of root-span elements for indices in the base. Take the dual f' restricted to M₀ and a root-positive form B (posRootForm) whose posForm on M₀ is positive definite. Using the baseOf pairwise pairing ≤ 0 lemma converted to statements about B.posForm, one applies LinearMap.BilinForm.linearIndependent_of_pairwise_le_zero — a standard criterion: if a symmetric bilinear form is positive definite on diagonal and pairwise off-diagonal ≤ 0 and the dual functional is positive on each vector, then the vectors are linearly independent. The Lean proof mirrors this: it builds B, proves the positivity hp and the pairwise nonpositivity hn by rewriting pairingIn via algebraMap_pairingIn' and baseOf_pairwise_pairing_le_zero, and finishes by calling the BilinForm lemma.

declarations.name: RootPairing.linearIndepOn_root_baseOf
declarations.nl_statement: For P a root system over a field R with P.IsCrystallographic and a rational dual f with nonzero values on roots, the subset baseOf P.root (f : M →+ ℚ) is linearly independent over R (the ground field), and its cardinality equals the rank.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The proof first applies the previous S-version with S = ℚ to get linear independence over ℚ of the corresponding root-span vectors, then uses finite-dimensional linear algebra (span and finrank arguments) to lift linear independence to R. Key steps: show the ℚ-span of the chosen vectors equals the root span (minimality/closure lemma using AddSubgroup closure of indecomposables), deduce the cardinality equals the finrank of the root span via choosing a ℚ-basis, then convert to R-linear independence by comparing finranks under scalar extension (span_span_of_tower and finrank computations). The Lean proof is longer but follows the standard algebraic-number-field-change-of-scalars argument directly; it uses Basis.mk and finrank equalities.

declarations.name: RootPairing.IsValuedIn.algebraMap_pairingIn'
declarations.nl_statement: If a RootPairing P is valued both in T and in S (S↪R faithfully) and T→S→R form a scalar tower, then applying algebraMap T→S to pairingIn T yields pairingIn S.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Inject algebraMap S→R via FaithfulSMul.algebraMap_injective, rewrite the composed algebraMap equality using IsScalarTower.algebraMap_eq and RingHom composition, and simplify. The Lean proof is a direct formalization of checking compatibility of chosen representatives for pairingIn under base change.

declarations.name: RootPairing.pairingIn_rat
declarations.nl_statement: If P is crystallographic and R is a ℚ-algebra, then pairingIn ℚ equals pairingIn ℤ (the integer pairing regarded in ℚ).
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: This follows by specializing algebraMap_pairingIn' to T = ℚ and S = ℤ and using simp to collapse the algebra maps: essentially algebraMap maps the integer representative into ℚ giving the same rational representative. The Lean proof is a one-line `simp` using algebraMap_pairingIn'.

declarations.name: RootPairing.RootPositiveForm.posForm_apply_root_root_le_zero_iff
declarations.nl_statement: For a root-positive form B taking values in an ordered ring S, the posForm applied to root i and root j is ≤ 0 iff the S-valued pairingIn i j ≤ 0.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: This is a direct companion to the zero-< version: it is obtained by rewriting the le-inequality into negations and applying the previously proved equivalence for strict positivity; the proof is a short manipulation using not_iff_not and the strict inequality lemma `zero_lt_apply_root_root_iff`.

pr_summary: Use the `grind` tactic / add `grind` annotations to simplify several short proofs: SimpleGraph.adj_of_mem_walk_support, Walk.support_cons (attr only), Finset.max_insert (attr only), Finset.mem_of_max, and Set.uIoc_of_le/uIoc_of_ge (attrs only), and simplify Set.eq_of_notMem_uIoc_of_notMem_uIoc using `grind`.

declarations.name: SimpleGraph.adj_of_mem_walk_support
declarations.nl_statement: For a nonempty walk p in a simple graph G, any vertex x in p.support has a neighbor y in p.support; i.e. there exists y ∈ p.support with G.Adj x y.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Induct on the walk p. The nil case is impossible because p is nonempty. For a cons h p' walk there are three subcases handled by case analysis on whether x is the head, whether the walk has length one, or whether x lies in the tail. If x equals the head u, take the next vertex v and use h. If the walk has length one pick the other endpoint and use symmetry of adjacency. Otherwise apply the induction hypothesis to the tail and lift the adjacency back to the full support. The proof in the PR runs these routine case splits and small rewrites via the `grind` tactic.
declarations.divergence: Uses standard induction and case analysis; the automated `grind` replaces explicit case and rewrite steps but follows the straightforward mathematical argument closely (low divergence).

declarations.name: Finset.mem_of_max
declarations.nl_statement: If s.max = a (where s.max : WithBot α) then a ∈ s.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: By finset induction: the empty case is impossible. For s = insert b t, compare the value of the max: either it comes from b or from the rest of the set. If the max equals b we are done. Otherwise it equals the max of t, and induction yields membership. The PR replaces a manual case split and uses `grind` (with WithBot.coe_eq_coe) to discharge the routine distinctions about coercions into WithBot.
declarations.divergence: Mathematical content identical; `grind` hides the explicit branching on whether the inserted element attains the maximum, but the argument is direct (small divergence).

declarations.name: Set.eq_of_notMem_uIoc_of_notMem_uIoc
declarations.nl_statement: In a distributive lattice / linear order setting, given a ≤ c and b ≤ c, if a ∉ Ι b c and b ∉ Ι a c then a = b.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Unpack the `notMem_uIoc` conditions into the corresponding inequalities, then perform a case analysis on the four possible disjuncts to derive le_antisymm a ≤ b and b ≤ a (or contradictions), concluding a = b. The PR replaces the explicit case splitting and elementwise inequality reasoning by invoking `grind` to discharge these routine inequality manipulations and contradictions.
declarations.divergence: The automated proof is a straightforward compression of the explicit inequality case analysis; it mirrors the mathematical plan but hides the low-level branching and small contradictions (moderate-low divergence).

pr_summary: Add lemmas establishing ⌊π⌋ = 3, ⌈π⌉ = 4, and round π = 3 using existing numeric bounds on π.

declarations.name: Real.floor_pi_eq_three
declarations.nl_statement: The floor of π is 3 (⌊π⌋ = 3).
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Uses Int.floor_eq_iff which says ⌊x⌋ = n ↔ n ≤ x ∧ x < n+1. The proof supplies the two inequalities 3 ≤ π (from the existing lemma pi_gt_three) and π < 4 (from pi_lt_four). A trivial numeric simplification (norm_num) is used to normalize the successor 3+1 = 4.

declarations.name: Real.ceil_pi_eq_four
declarations.nl_statement: The ceiling of π is 4 (⌈π⌉ = 4).
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Uses Int.ceil_eq_iff which says ⌈x⌉ = n ↔ n-1 < x ∧ x ≤ n. For n = 4 the proof discharges the two inequalities 3 < π (pi_gt_three) and π ≤ 4 (pi_lt_four.le). A norm_num call handles the arithmetic n-1 = 3.

declarations.name: Real.round_pi_eq_three
declarations.nl_statement: The nearest integer (rounding to the nearest integer) of π is 3 (round π = 3).
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Relies on the identity round x = ⌊x + 1/2⌋ (round_eq) and then proves ⌊π + 1/2⌋ = 3 using Int.floor_eq_iff: show 3 ≤ π + 1/2 and π + 1/2 < 4. These follow directly from the established bounds 3 < π (pi_gt_three) and a decimal upper bound on π (pi_lt_d2 gives π < 3.15, hence π + 1/2 < 3.65 < 4). Small numeric simplifications (norm_num) and rewriting with the known bounds finish the two goals. The proof is a straightforward formalization of the usual numeric rounding argument.

pr_summary: Rename several Submodule/orthogonal projection lemmas for clearer names and update references. Added/renamed theorems relating orthogonalProjection and starProjection to linearProjOfIsCompl and adjusted uses in Positive.lean.

declarations.name: LinearMap.IsSymmetricProjection.le_iff_range_le_range
declarations.nl_statement: For symmetric idempotent linear maps (symmetric projections) p and q, we have p ≤ q (in the Loewner order) if and only if range p ≤ range q.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Unpack `p ≤ q` as `(q - p).IsPositive`. For symmetric projections one can express the real part of ⟪T a, a⟫ as the squared norm of T a, so the positivity condition reduces to a norm inequality between p and q applied to a vector a in the range of p. Translating that inequality into the submodule membership condition uses the characterization of `q` as the star-projection of its range and the norm/minimality properties of star-projections; the updated proof simply uses the renamed lemma identifying the star-projection's linear map with the projection coming from the `IsCompl` structure of range q.

declarations.name: Submodule.orthogonalProjection_apply_eq_linearProjOfIsCompl
declarations.nl_statement: If K admits an orthogonal projection, then for any x, K.orthogonalProjection x equals the linear projection of x given by the `IsCompl K Kᗮ` decomposition (i.e., linearProjOfIsCompl applied with the complement Kᗮ).
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Use that K and its orthogonal complement are an `IsCompl` pair. Rewrite x using the decomposition `IsCompl.projection_add_projection_eq_self` and evaluate both sides componentwise: the K-component of the `IsCompl` linear projection is the orthogonal projection (by `orthogonalProjection_mem_subspace_eq_self`), and the Kᗮ-component is zero (by `orthogonalProjection_mem_subspace_orthogonalComplement_eq_zero`). This yields the equality of the two maps on each x.

declarations.name: Submodule.coe_orthogonalProjection_eq_linearProjOfIsCompl
declarations.nl_statement: As linear maps, (K.orthogonalProjection : E →ₗ[𝕜] K) equals K.linearProjOfIsCompl _ (isCompl_orthogonal_of_hasOrthogonalProjection).
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: This is an immediate consequence of the pointwise equality from `orthogonalProjection_apply_eq_linearProjOfIsCompl`; the proof is a `LinearMap.ext` using that theorem.

declarations.name: Submodule.coe_starProjection_eq_isComplProjection
declarations.nl_statement: For K admitting an orthogonal projection, the linear map underlying K.starProjection equals the `projection` map associated to the `IsCompl K Kᗮ` structure (i.e., the isCompl projection from the decomposition).
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Unfold `starProjection` and use `coe_orthogonalProjection_eq_linearProjOfIsCompl` together with the general `IsCompl.projection` definition; the proof is achieved by a `simp` that applies the renamed lemma and `IsCompl.projection`.

declarations.name: Submodule.starProjection_le_starProjection_iff
declarations.nl_statement: For complete submodules U and V admitting orthogonal projections, U.starProjection ≤ V.starProjection iff U ≤ V (order on star-projection operators corresponds to inclusion of submodules).
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Translate the inequality between starProjection operators into the corresponding linear-map inequality (`coe_le_coe_iff`) and then use that `isSymmetricProjection_starProjection` and the `le_iff_range_le_range` lemma for symmetric projections reduce the statement to a range inclusion. The proof uses the renamed equality `coe_starProjection_eq_isComplProjection` to relate the star-projection linear maps to the `IsCompl` projection and then `IsCompl.projection_range` to finish.

pr_summary: Add basic monotonicity/sign lemmas for ArchimedeanClass.stdPart and tighten visibility on an internal lemma used for ordering the residue field.

declarations.name: ArchimedeanClass.FiniteResidueField.ordConnected_preimage_mk'
declarations.nl_statement: For every x in the residue field, the preimage under the quotient map (Quotient.mk of the maximal-ideal quotient) of the singleton {x} is order-connected (i.e. any two points in the preimage have the whole interval between them contained in the preimage).
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Unpack the definitions: given two representatives y ≤ z in the preimage of the same residue class, their difference lies in the maximal ideal, which by the residue ideal characterization rewrites as a nonunit condition. Translate that condition into an inequality about ArchimedeanClass.mk using FiniteElement.not_isUnit_iff_mk_pos. From this inequality and the antitone/monotone behaviour of the map mk (expressed by mk_antitoneOn) one shows any intermediate element stays in the same fiber. The proof is a short chain of rewrites and an application of mk_antitoneOn.

declarations.name: ArchimedeanClass.stdPart_nonneg
declarations.nl_statement: If 0 ≤ x in K, then 0 ≤ stdPart x.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Split on whether the residue class ArchimedeanClass.mk x is zero. If it is zero then the definition of stdPart uses the OrderRingHom coming from the residue-field embedding, and monotonicity of that map yields 0 ≤ stdPart x. If the residue class is nonzero then stdPart x = 0 by the already-proved characterization stdPart_eq_zero, so the inequality holds. This is a direct case analysis mirroring the mathematical argument.

declarations.name: ArchimedeanClass.stdPart_nonpos
declarations.nl_statement: If x ≤ 0 in K, then stdPart x ≤ 0.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Apply stdPart_nonneg to -x (which is ≥ 0) and use stdPart_neg (stdPart (-x) = -stdPart x) to conclude stdPart x ≤ 0. The Lean proof is a one-line reduction using these lemmas.

declarations.name: ArchimedeanClass.add (instance)
declarations.nl_statement: Defines addition on ArchimedeanClass R by mk(x) + mk(y) := mk(x * y). The instance supplies the proof that this is well-defined (respects the ArchimedeanClass ordering) required by lift₂.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: To show the lifted binary operation is well-defined we must prove that if mk x₁ ≤ mk x₂ and mk y₁ ≤ mk y₂ then mk(x₁ * y₁) = mk(x₂ * y₂). The code shows two inequalities: using the helper lemma mk_mul_le_of_le with the given ≤ hypotheses we get mk(x₁*x₁') ≤ mk(x₂*y₂), and applying the same lemma to the reversed ≥ hypotheses yields the opposite inequality; antisymmetry gives equality. The Lean proof hooks these together directly using antisymm.
declarations.divergence: None significant — the proof is a direct formalization of the mathematical argument using the auxiliary lemma mk_mul_le_of_le and antisymmetry.

declarations.name: ArchimedeanClass.mk_div
declarations.nl_statement: For a field R, mk (x / y) = mk x - mk y.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Simple computation using field identities: rewrite x / y as x * y⁻¹, then use the definitions mk(x*y)=mk x + mk y and mk(y⁻¹) = - mk y, and rewrite subtraction as addition of the negation. The Lean proof performs these rewrites in three steps (div_eq_mul_inv, mk_mul, mk_inv) and finishes with sub_eq_add_neg.
declarations.divergence: None — the proof is an immediate chain of definitional rewrites reflecting the straightforward algebraic identity.

declarations.name: ArchimedeanClass.noncomputable instance : LinearOrderedAddCommGroupWithTop (field case)
declarations.nl_statement: Provides the structure of a LinearOrderedAddCommGroupWithTop on ArchimedeanClass R when R is a field and ordered; in particular supplies zsmul_succ' (the relation (n+1)•x = n•x + x for integer scalar multiplication) and other zsmul fields.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: All required zsmul properties are proved separately (e.g. zsmul_succ' is proved by case analysis on x and using zpow identities). The instance fields then reference these lemmas; in particular the zsmul_succ' instance field is set by `by exact zsmul_succ'`, which merely forwards to the already proven lemma. The rest of the instance also directly uses the previously established lemmas (zsmul_zero', zsmul_neg', etc.)

declarations.name: LinearOrderedAddCommGroupWithTop.add_left_injective_of_ne_top
declarations.nl_statement: If b ≠ ⊤, the map x ↦ x + b is injective.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: If x + b = y + b, subtract b from both sides to get x = y. The proof in Lean performs this cancellation by applying congr (i.e. subtracting b) and simplifying using add_neg_cancel_of_ne_top (which requires b ≠ ⊤).

declarations.name: LinearOrderedAddCommGroupWithTop.add_right_injective_of_ne_top
declarations.nl_statement: If b ≠ ⊤, the map x ↦ b + x is injective.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Reduce to the left-addition case using commutativity of addition: b + x = b + y ↔ x + b = y + b, then apply add_left_injective_of_ne_top.

declarations.name: LinearOrderedAddCommGroupWithTop.add_left_inj_of_ne_top
declarations.nl_statement: (simp) For a ≠ ⊤, b + a = c + a ↔ b = c.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: This is the eq_iff form of injectivity: use (add_left_injective_of_ne_top _ h).eq_iff.

declarations.name: LinearOrderedAddCommGroupWithTop.add_right_inj_of_ne_top
declarations.nl_statement: (simp) For a ≠ ⊤, a + b = a + c ↔ b = c.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Analogous to the left version: take eq_iff of add_right_injective_of_ne_top.

declarations.name: LinearOrderedAddCommGroupWithTop.sub_left_injective_of_ne_top
declarations.nl_statement: If b ≠ ⊤, the map x ↦ x - b is injective.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Rewrite subtraction as addition of the negation: x - b = x + (-b). Then apply add_left_injective_of_ne_top to (-b), using that -b ≠ ⊤ (proved by a short simp).

declarations.name: LinearOrderedAddCommGroupWithTop.sub_right_injective_of_ne_top
declarations.nl_statement: If b ≠ ⊤, the map x ↦ b - x is injective.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Write b - x as b + (-x) and compose the injective map x ↦ b + x with negation (which is injective). Conclude injectivity by composing known injective maps.

declarations.name: LinearOrderedAddCommGroupWithTop.sub_left_inj_of_ne_top
declarations.nl_statement: (simp) For a ≠ ⊤, b - a = c - a ↔ b = c.

declarations.name: LinearOrderedAddCommGroupWithTop.sub_right_inj_of_ne_top
declarations.nl_statement: (simp) For a ≠ ⊤, a - b = a - c ↔ b = c.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Take eq_iff of sub_right_injective_of_ne_top.

declarations.name: LinearOrderedAddCommGroupWithTop.add_left_strictMono_of_ne_top
declarations.nl_statement: If b ≠ ⊤, the function x ↦ x + b is strictly monotone.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Start from monotonicity of adding a constant (Monotone.add_const monotone_id). Then use the general fact strictMono_of_injective: a monotone map that is injective is strictly monotone. Apply add_left_injective_of_ne_top for injectivity.

declarations.name: LinearOrderedAddCommGroupWithTop.add_right_strictMono_of_ne_top
declarations.nl_statement: If b ≠ ⊤, the function x ↦ b + x is strictly monotone.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Reduce to the left-addition strict monotonicity via commutativity of addition and apply add_left_strictMono_of_ne_top.

declarations.name: LinearOrderedAddCommGroupWithTop.add_lt_add_iff_left_of_ne_top
declarations.nl_statement: (simp) For a ≠ ⊤, b + a < c + a ↔ b < c.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: A strictly monotone map preserves and reflects strict inequality; use (add_left_strictMono_of_ne_top _ h).lt_iff_lt to get the iff.

declarations.name: LinearOrderedAddCommGroupWithTop.add_lt_add_iff_right_of_ne_top
declarations.nl_statement: (simp) For a ≠ ⊤, a + b < a + c ↔ b < c.

declarations.name: LinearOrderedAddCommGroupWithTop.add_le_add_iff_left_of_ne_top
declarations.nl_statement: (simp) For a ≠ ⊤, b + a ≤ c + a ↔ b ≤ c.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Analogous to the strict case, using le_iff_le from the strictMono instance (strict monotone maps reflect ≤ as well).

declarations.name: LinearOrderedAddCommGroupWithTop.add_le_add_iff_right_of_ne_top
declarations.nl_statement: (simp) For a ≠ ⊤, a + b ≤ a + c ↔ b ≤ c.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Analogous to the left version via add_right_strictMono_of_ne_top.

declarations.name: LinearOrderedAddCommGroupWithTop.sub_left_strictMono_of_ne_top
declarations.nl_statement: If b ≠ ⊤, the map x ↦ x - b is strictly monotone.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Rewrite x - b as x + (-b) and reuse add_left_strictMono_of_ne_top applied to -b (showing -b ≠ ⊤ by simp), as in the injective case.

declarations.name: LinearOrderedAddCommGroupWithTop.sub_lt_sub_iff_left_of_ne_top
declarations.nl_statement: (simp) For a ≠ ⊤, b - a < c - a ↔ b < c.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Take lt_iff_lt of sub_left_strictMono_of_ne_top.

declarations.name: LinearOrderedAddCommGroupWithTop.sub_le_sub_iff_left_of_ne_top
declarations.nl_statement: (simp) For a ≠ ⊤, b - a ≤ c - a ↔ b ≤ c.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Take le_iff_le of sub_left_strictMono_of_ne_top.

declarations.name: LinearOrderedAddCommGroupWithTop.sub_pos
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Case split on whether b = ⊤. If b = ⊤ the left side simplifies to 0 < a - ⊤ = 0 < ⊤ which holds, matching the RHS case b = ⊤. If b ≠ ⊤, rewrite using sub_self_eq_zero_of_ne_top and reduce to the corresponding strict inequality via the strict monotonicity of adding -b (implemented by sub_left_strictMono_of_ne_top applied to -b). The Lean proof does the straightforward case split and simplification.

pr_summary: Add lemma relating HasDetPlusMinusOne to absolute value of determinant and a small Units lemma; simplify instance proof to use the new characterization.

declarations.name: Units.val_eq_neg_one
declarations.nl_statement: For a unit a in a ring, its coercion to the ring equals -1 if and only if the unit equals -1: (a : α) = -1 ↔ a = -1.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Rewrite the goal using Units.coe_neg_one to replace -1 on the unit side by its coercion, turning (a : α) = -1 into (a : α) = ((-1 : αˣ) : α). Then apply val_inj (injectivity of Units.coe) to deduce a = -1. The proof in the file is exactly: rw [← Units.coe_neg_one, val_inj].

declarations.name: hasDetPlusMinusOne_iff_abs_det
declarations.nl_statement: A subgroup Γ has determinant ±1 for all its elements (HasDetPlusMinusOne Γ) iff for every g ∈ Γ the absolute value of g.det.val equals 1, i.e. HasDetPlusMinusOne Γ ↔ ∀ {g}, g ∈ Γ → |g.det.val| = 1.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The forward direction is the existing lemma HasDetPlusMinusOne.abs_det. For the converse, assume ∀ g ∈ Γ, |g.det.val| = 1. From |x| = 1 one can infer x = 1 ∨ x = -1 (using abs_eq with appropriate side-conditions and unfolding GeneralLinearGroup.val_det_apply), so apply that to g.det.val to obtain the disjunction required by HasDetPlusMinusOne. The file proves this compactly with simpa using abs_eq and the unfolding of val_det. In short: convert absolute-value-one to the ±1 disjunction and package into the HasDetPlusMinusOne constructor.

declarations.name: instance (Γ : Subgroup (GL (Fin 2) ℝ)) [Γ.IsArithmetic] : HasDetPlusMinusOne Γ
declarations.nl_statement: For any arithmetic subgroup Γ of GL(2, ℝ), Γ satisfies HasDetPlusMinusOne (i.e., every element has determinant ±1).
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The proof now begins by rewriting the goal using hasDetPlusMinusOne_iff_abs_det, reducing it to proving ∀ g ∈ Γ, |g.det.val| = 1. Given g ∈ Γ, use the commensurability property of arithmetic subgroups to find n > 0 with g^n ∈ the integral model image, then show |(g.det^n).val| = 1 (since determinants of integral matrices have value ±1), rewrite |(g.det^n).val| as |g.det.val|^n and deduce |g.det.val| = 1 from |x|^n = 1. The file uses simpa and abs_pow to finish. This follows the standard arithmetic-group argument: pass to a power lying in the integral subgroup, use integrality to force determinant ±1, then take nth roots in absolute value.

pr_summary: Weaken assumptions in Schwarz lemma: replace assumptions that f maps an open ball to an open ball by mapping to the corresponding closed ball, and adapt proofs accordingly. Minor refactors: make schwarz_aux private and place declarations in Complex namespace.

declarations.name: Complex.schwarz_aux
declarations.nl_statement: For f : ℂ → ℂ differentiable on the open ball ball(c,R₁), if f maps that open ball into the closed ball centered at f c of radius R₂, then for any z in ball(c,R₁) the slope norm ‖dslope f c z‖ ≤ R₂ / R₁.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Fix z in the ball and choose r<R₁ with z in ball(c,r). Use continuity properties of the dslope on the closure of the smaller ball (DifferentiableOn.diffContOnCl) to reduce the inequality at z to an inequality on the frontier sphere of radius r. On the frontier, compute dslope explicitly (using dslope_of_ne and slope_def_module) and compare its norm to R₂/r; the mapsTo hypothesis into the closed ball is used to bound the numerator by R₂ via mem_closedBall_iff_norm. Finally let r→R₁ from below to conclude the R₂/R₁ bound.

declarations.name: Complex.norm_dslope_le_div_of_mapsTo_ball
declarations.nl_statement: If f : ℂ → E is differentiable on ball(c,R₁) and maps ball(c,R₁) into closedBall(f c,R₂), then for any z∈ball(c,R₁) we have ‖dslope f c z‖ ≤ R₂ / R₁.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Handle the zero dslope case separately. For nonzero dslope pick a norm-one dual functional g (exists_dual_vector) so that composing with g reduces to the scalar case g∘f : ℂ→ℂ. Apply the auxiliary scalar lemma (schwarz_aux) to g∘f; to apply it we need that g maps the image closed ball into a closed disk in ℂ, which follows from the Lipschitz property of g (norm one) producing mapsTo_closedBall. Take care with the nonnegativity of R₂ (use nonempty_closedBall.mp).

declarations.name: Complex.affine_of_mapsTo_ball_of_exists_norm_dslope_eq_div
declarations.nl_statement: In the setup of the previous theorem, if there exists z₀∈ball(c,R₁) with equality ‖dslope f c z₀‖ = R₂ / R₁, then f is affine on ball(c,R₁): f(z)=f c + (z-c) • dslope f c z₀.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: From the global bound on ‖dslope f c z‖ (norm_dslope_le_div_of_mapsTo_ball) and the equality at z₀, infer that norm∘(dslope f c) attains a maximum at z₀. Using differentiability of the dslope and the maximum principle for norms (eqOn_of_isPreconnected_of_isMaxOn_norm) on the convex ball, deduce dslope f c is constant on the ball and conclude the affine formula.

declarations.name: Complex.affine_of_mapsTo_ball_of_exists_norm_dslope_eq_div'
declarations.nl_statement: Variant: if there exists some z₀ with ‖dslope f c z₀‖ = R₂ / R₁ then there exists C with ‖C‖ = R₂ / R₁ and f(z)=f c + (z-c) • C on ball(c,R₁).
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Extract the witness z₀ and apply the previous theorem to produce the desired constant C = dslope f c z₀ and the equality of norms and EqOn property.

declarations.name: Complex.norm_deriv_le_div_of_mapsTo_ball
declarations.nl_statement: If f : ℂ → E is differentiable on ball(c,R₁) and maps that ball into closedBall(f c,R₂), with R₁>0, then ‖deriv f c‖ ≤ R₂ / R₁.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Specialize the dslope bound at z=c (mem_ball_self) and use dslope_same = deriv to get the desired inequality.

declarations.name: Complex.dist_le_div_mul_dist_of_mapsTo_ball
declarations.nl_statement: Under the same hypotheses as the dslope theorem, for any z ∈ ball(c,R₁) we have dist(f z, f c) ≤ (R₂ / R₁) * dist(z,c).
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: If z=c the inequality is trivial. Otherwise rewrite the left side in terms of dslope and apply norm_dslope_le_div_of_mapsTo_ball, rearranging to the stated form using dist_eq_norm and basic algebra (dividing by dist z c).

declarations.name: Complex.norm_deriv_le_one_of_mapsTo_ball
declarations.nl_statement: Special case for self-maps of a disk: if f maps ball(c,R) into closedBall(f c,R) with R>0, then ‖deriv f c‖ ≤ 1.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Apply norm_deriv_le_div_of_mapsTo_ball with R₁=R and R₂=R; then simplify R/R = 1 using div_self (since R>0).

declarations.name: Complex.dist_le_dist_of_mapsTo_ball_self
declarations.nl_statement: If f maps ball(c,R) into closedBall(f c,R), then for any z∈ball(c,R) we have dist (f z) (f c) ≤ dist z c.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: This is a direct corollary of dist_le_div_mul_dist_of_mapsTo_ball with R₂=R and noting R/R=1; small bookkeeping ensures the nonzero radius condition is satisfied implicitly.

declarations.name: Complex.norm_le_norm_of_mapsTo_ball_self
declarations.nl_statement: If f : ℂ → E is differentiable on ball(0,R) and maps ball(0,R) into closedBall(0,R) and f 0 = 0, then for any z with ‖z‖<R we have ‖f z‖ ≤ ‖z‖.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Rewrite the goal as dist(f z,0) ≤ dist(z,0) and apply dist_le_dist_of_mapsTo_ball_self to the map f with the center adjusted by f 0 = 0; convert the membership ‖z‖<R to z∈ball(0,R) as needed.

pr_summary: Add lemmas describing how iteratedDeriv behaves under translations by subtraction: two new lemmas iteratedDeriv_comp_sub_const and iteratedDeriv_comp_const_sub; also refactor shift_invariance lemmas to use top-level variables (n, f, s).

declarations.name: iteratedDeriv_comp_const_add
declarations.nl_statement: For all n, f, s, the n-th iterated derivative of the function z ↦ f(s + z) equals the function t ↦ iteratedDeriv n f (s + t).
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Proof by induction on n. For n=0 the statement is trivial from the definition. For the successor case, apply the inductive hypothesis to reduce to deriv of the (n)-th iterated derivative; use funext and the lemma deriv_comp_const_add which says deriv (g ∘ (λz, s + z)) = (deriv g) ∘ (λz, s + z).
declarations.divergence: Direct formalisation of the math; proof mirrors the natural induction and uses the expected deriv_comp_const_add lemma.

declarations.name: iteratedDeriv_comp_add_const
declarations.nl_statement: For all n, f, s, the n-th iterated derivative of z ↦ f(z + s) equals t ↦ iteratedDeriv n f (t + s).
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Identical shape to the previous lemma: induction on n, base case trivial; inductive step uses funext and deriv_comp_add_const to commute derivation with right-translation.
declarations.divergence: Direct and transparent; matches the usual mathematical proof.

declarations.name: iteratedDeriv_comp_sub_const
declarations.nl_statement: For all n, f, s, iteratedDeriv n (λ z, f (z - s)) = λ t, iteratedDeriv n f (t - s).
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Induction on n. Base n=0 is immediate. For the successor, the inductive hypothesis gives the identity for the inner iterated derivative; one then applies funext and the lemma deriv_comp_sub_const (which states how deriv behaves under post-composition by subtracting a constant on the right) to conclude.
declarations.divergence: Very close to the textbook argument. The proof uses an underscore for an auxiliary differentiability argument (a standard Lean pattern); otherwise it follows the math directly.

declarations.name: iteratedDeriv_comp_const_sub
declarations.nl_statement: For all n, f, s, iteratedDeriv n (λ z, f (s - z)) = λ t, (-1 : 𝕜)^n • iteratedDeriv n f (s - t).
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Expected proof: induction on n. Base case holds by definition. For the successor, use the inductive hypothesis to express the n-th iterated derivative composed with negation up to a factor (-1)^n, then use deriv rules for composition with (s - ·) (which is translation composed with negation) and for scalar multiplication by (-1) on functions, to obtain an extra factor of -1 at each step, yielding (-1)^{n+1}.
declarations.divergence: The file contains an incomplete/erroneous proof: after rewriting with deriv_fun_const_smul' and deriv_comp_const_sub the proof ends with an isolated token `module`. The intended mathematical argument is clear, but the Lean proof as committed is not finished and will not compile; it needs a short completion (replacing `module` with the correct sequence of rewrites/tactics to arrange smuls and powers).

pr_summary: Clean up Rayleigh quotient file: add rayleighQuotient_add, tighten a scalar expression in scaling lemma, replace a non-terminal simp by simpa, and remove a number of unnecessary explicit coercions in statements.

declarations.name: ContinuousLinearMap.rayleighQuotient_add
declarations.nl_statement: For continuous linear maps T and S and any vector x, the Rayleigh quotient is additive: (T+S).rayleighQuotient x = T.rayleighQuotient x + S.rayleighQuotient x.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Unfold the definition of rayleighQuotient and use linearity of the inner product in the left slot: reApplyInnerSelf (T+S) x = re ⟪(T+S) x, x⟫ = re(⟪T x, x⟫ + ⟪S x, x⟫) = re ⟪T x, x⟫ + re ⟪S x, x⟫, then divide by ‖x‖^2 and use add_div. In Lean this is a one-line simp using reApplyInnerSelf_apply, inner_add_left and add_div.
declarations.divergence: The formal proof is a direct, literal reflection of the mathematical argument; no noteworthy divergence.

declarations.name: ContinuousLinearMap.image_rayleigh_eq_image_rayleigh_sphere
declarations.nl_statement: For r>0, the image of the nonzero vectors under the Rayleigh quotient equals the image of the sphere of radius r: rayleighQuotient T '' {0}ᶜ = rayleighQuotient T '' sphere 0 r.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Given a nonzero x, scale it to lie on the sphere by c = ‖x‖⁻¹ * r (a nonzero scalar). Then use rayleigh_smul to show the Rayleigh quotient is invariant under nonzero scalars, so the value at x equals the value at c • x on the sphere. The reverse inclusion uses that points on the sphere are nonzero. The Lean proof implements exactly these steps (explicit construction of c, checking it is nonzero, simp for norms and invariance, and trivial reverse direction).
declarations.divergence: Very close to the informal argument; the only change in the PR was a minor tightening of the scalar expression's type (no change in the math).

declarations.name: IsSelfAdjoint.eq_smul_self_of_isLocalExtrOn_real
declarations.nl_statement: (Real case) If T is self-adjoint on a real inner-product space and x₀ is a local extremum of T.reApplyInnerSelf on the sphere of radius ‖x₀‖, then T x₀ is a scalar multiple of x₀; specifically T x₀ = (T.rayleighQuotient x₀) • x₀.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Use the Lagrange multipliers (IsLocalExtrOn.exists_multipliers...) applied to T.reApplyInnerSelf and the constraint ‖x‖^2 = ‖x₀‖^2 to obtain real multipliers a,b with a • x₀ + b • T x₀ = 0. Rules out the trivial b=0 case, then solve for T x₀ = c • x₀ with c = -b⁻¹ a. Finally take inner product with x₀ and rewrite to identify the scalar c with the Rayleigh quotient re ⟪T x₀, x₀⟫ / ‖x₀‖^2. The Lean proof follows these steps: obtains multipliers, handles cases, computes c, and uses congr_arg and simpa to finish. The PR replaced a short sequence of congr_arg + simp + exact by a single simpa, a purely syntactic cleanup.
declarations.divergence: Faithful to the mathematical Lagrange multiplier argument. The PR's modification is only a local cleanup (simpa vs separate steps); no mathematical change.

declarations.name: IsSelfAdjoint.eq_smul_self_of_isLocalExtrOn
declarations.nl_statement: (General RCLike 𝕜) If T is self-adjoint and x₀ is a local extremum of T.reApplyInnerSelf on the sphere, then T x₀ = (T.rayleighQuotient x₀ : 𝕜) • x₀ (the Rayleigh quotient interpreted in 𝕜).
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Reduce to the real case by viewing the RCLike scalar field as a real inner-product space via the rclikeToReal construction and restricting scalars. Then apply the real theorem (eq_smul_self_of_isLocalExtrOn_real) to conclude. The Lean proof sets up the rclike-to-real instance and calls the real case; the PR only adjusted syntactic coercions of the Rayleigh-quotient cast to 𝕜.
declarations.divergence: Direct reduction to the real case; the modification is syntactic (coercion style) only.

declarations.name: IsSelfAdjoint.hasEigenvector_of_isLocalExtrOn
declarations.nl_statement: If T is self-adjoint and x₀ ≠ 0 is a local extremum of the Rayleigh quotient on a sphere, then x₀ is an eigenvector of T with eigenvalue T.rayleighQuotient x₀.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The theorem is immediate from eq_smul_self_of_isLocalExtrOn: the latter gives T x₀ = λ • x₀ with λ the Rayleigh quotient, which by rewriting is exactly the statement that x₀ is in the eigenspace for λ. The Lean proof just applies the previous theorem and wraps it with HasEigenvector/Module.End.mem_eigenspace_iff; the PR removed an unnecessary explicit coercion in the eigenvalue expression.
declarations.divergence: The formal proof is a trivial unfolding of the mathematical statement; the PR only adjusted notation/coercion.

declarations.name: IsSelfAdjoint.hasEigenvector_of_isMaxOn
declarations.nl_statement: If T is self-adjoint and x₀ ≠ 0 is a global maximum point (on a given sphere) of T.reApplyInnerSelf, then x₀ is an eigenvector and the corresponding eigenvalue equals the global supremum of the Rayleigh quotient (interpreted as a real number).
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Localize the global maximum to a local extremum and reuse hasEigenvector_of_isLocalExtrOn. Then identify the eigenvalue as the iSup over all nonzero vectors by equating the supremum over nonzero vectors with the supremum over the fixed sphere (image_rayleigh_eq_image_rayleigh_sphere and iSup_rayleigh_eq_iSup_rayleigh_sphere), and use IsMaxOn.iSup_eq to show the local maximum value equals the global supremum. The Lean proof follows these steps; the PR primarily adjusted the displayed eigenvalue to be given without an unnecessary coercion notation and used existing lemmas (iSup equality) to finish.
declarations.divergence: Follows the standard argument; changes are not mathematical but formatting/coercion-related.

declarations.name: IsSelfAdjoint.hasEigenvector_of_isMinOn
declarations.nl_statement: Analogously, if x₀ ≠ 0 is a global minimum point on a sphere, then x₀ is an eigenvector and the eigenvalue equals the global infimum of the Rayleigh quotient (as a real).
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Same strategy as for the maximum case: reduce to the local extremum case, use the equality of iInf on the set of nonzero vectors with iInf on the chosen sphere, and apply IsMinOn.iInf_eq. The Lean proof mirrors this exactly; PR changes are syntactic/coercion cleanups.
declarations.divergence: Direct formalization of the mathematical proof; only cosmetic changes in the PR.

declarations.name: LinearMap.IsSymmetric.hasEigenvalue_iSup_of_finiteDimensional
declarations.nl_statement: For a symmetric linear map T on a nontrivial finite-dimensional 𝕜-vector space E, the supremum of the Rayleigh quotient over nonzero vectors is an eigenvalue of T.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Pick some nonzero vector to fix a sphere; in finite dimensions the sphere is compact and the continuous function re⟪T x,x⟫/‖x‖^2 attains a maximum on that sphere. That maximizer x₀ is nonzero, and by the previous IsSelfAdjoint.hasEigenvector_of_isMaxOn (applied to the self-adjoint form of T) it yields an eigenvector with eigenvalue equal to the supremum over nonzero vectors. The Lean proof constructs the compact sphere, applies existence of maxima/minima for continuous functions on compact sets, extracts x₀, checks nonzeroness, and applies the earlier eigenvector result. The PR only changed superficial coercion of the eigenvalue expression in the statement.
declarations.divergence: The formal proof tracks the textbook finite-dimensional compactness argument closely; only notation for the real-valued supremum was simplified in the PR.

declarations.name: LinearMap.IsSymmetric.hasEigenvalue_iInf_of_finiteDimensional
declarations.nl_statement: For symmetric T on a nontrivial finite-dimensional space, the infimum of the Rayleigh quotient over nonzero vectors is an eigenvalue of T.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Same as the supremum case but using existence of a minimum on the compact sphere and the corresponding IsSelfAdjoint.hasEigenvector_of_isMinOn. The Lean proof mirrors this approach; the PR again only altered superficial coercion in the statement.

pr_summary: Adds a few small lemmas about the intrinsic star on linear maps: two equalities expressing star as conjugation by the star linear equivalence, and two simp lemmas for the intrinsic star acting on toSpanSingleton and on smulRight.

declarations.name: LinearMap.intrinsicStar_eq_comp
declarations.nl_statement: For a linear map f : E →ₗ[R] F, the intrinsic star of f equals pre- and post-composition of f with the module-level star linear equivalence: star f = (starLinearEquiv R).toLinearMap ∘ₛₗ f ∘ₛₗ (starLinearEquiv R).toLinearMap.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: This is true by definition of the intrinsic star: (star f) x = star (f (star x)), which is exactly the effect of conjugating f by the linear map underlying the star equivalence. In Lean the theorem is proved by refl (rfl).

declarations.name: IntrinsicStar.starLinearEquiv_eq
declarations.nl_statement: The star linear equivalence on the function space equals the arrowCongr of the star linear equivalence: starLinearEquiv R (A := E →ₗ[R] F) = (starLinearEquiv R).arrowCongr (starLinearEquiv R).
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: This equality follows directly from the definitions: the star equivalence on the arrow type is exactly the arrowCongr construction applied to the scalar-module star; the Lean proof is rfl.

declarations.name: LinearMap.intrinsicStar_toSpanSingleton
declarations.nl_statement: For a semiring S and a : E, the intrinsic star of the linear map toSpanSingleton S E a is the linear map toSpanSingleton S E (star a): star (toSpanSingleton S E a) = toSpanSingleton S E (star a).
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Prove equality of linear maps by extensionality on an arbitrary argument and simplify: both sides send x to star (a • star x) which simp reduces to (star a) • x. The Lean proof is `by ext; simp`.

declarations.name: LinearMap.intrinsicStar_smulRight
declarations.nl_statement: For f : E →ₗ[S] S and x : F, the intrinsic star commutes with smulRight: star (f.smulRight x) = (star f).smulRight (star x).
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Again use extensionality and simplification: both sides evaluated at an argument yield the same scalar after `simp`. The Lean proof is `by ext; simp`.

declarations.name: SchwartzMap.smooth
declarations.nl_statement: For any Schwartz function f : 𝓢(E, F) and any regularity level n : ℕ∞, f is ContDiff of order n (i.e. f : ContDiff ℝ n).
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The structure SchwartzMap stores a field smooth' : ContDiff ℝ ∞ toFun. Since ∞ is the maximal regularity, use the fact that ContDiff ℝ ∞ implies ContDiff ℝ n by restricting regularity: apply the .of_le lemma with the instance that n ≤ ∞ (mod_cast le_top). This yields ContDiff ℝ n f.

declarations.name: SchwartzMap.contDiffAt
declarations.nl_statement: For any Schwartz function f : 𝓢(E, F), any regularity n : ℕ∞ and any point x : E, f is ContDiffAt of order n at x.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: From the global ContDiff statement (f.smooth n) obtain the corresponding pointwise version by taking .contDiffAt. That is, ContDiff ℝ n f implies ContDiffAt ℝ n f x for any x.

declarations.name: SchwartzMap.continuous
declarations.nl_statement: Every Schwartz function f : 𝓢(E, F) is continuous.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: ContDiff of order 0 is equivalent to continuity. Use the already proved smooth lemma at level 0, (f.smooth 0), and apply its .continuous projection to conclude Continuous f. (The declaration also carries the @[continuity] and @[fun_prop] attributes.)

declarations.name: SchwartzMap.differentiable
declarations.nl_statement: Every Schwartz function f : 𝓢(E, F) is differentiable (as a function from E to F).
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: A function is differentiable if it is ContDiff of order ≥ 1. From (f.smooth 1) we get ContDiff ℝ 1 f, and then use the .differentiable projection with one_ne_zero to obtain Differentiable ℝ f.

declarations.name: SchwartzMap.differentiableAt
declarations.nl_statement: Every Schwartz function f : 𝓢(E, F) is differentiable at every point x : E.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Differentability at a point follows from global differentiability: take f.differentiable and apply .differentiableAt to obtain DifferentiableAt ℝ f x for any x.

pr_summary: Remove the hypothesis that n ≠ 0 from Subgroup.closure_pow_le, making the lemma hold for n = 0 as well; adjust closure_pow to use the new lemma.

declarations.name: Subgroup.closure_pow_le
declarations.nl_statement: For every natural number n, the closure of the n-fold pointwise power of a set s is contained in the closure of s: closure (s ^ n) ≤ closure s.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Proof by induction on n. Base case n = 0: s^0 = {1}, so closure (s^0) is the trivial subgroup generated by 1, which is contained in closure s since 1 ∈ closure s; the code introduces an arbitrary x in closure (s^0), simplifies using pow_zero, and reduces to showing x = 1 and hence the inclusion. Inductive step: for n+1 rewrite s^(n+1) = s^n * s, apply closure_mul_le to get closure (s^n) ⊔ closure s, then use the inductive hypothesis closure (s^n) ≤ closure s to collapse the sup to closure s.

declarations.name: Subgroup.closure_pow
declarations.nl_statement: If 1 ∈ s and n ≠ 0, then the closure of the n-fold power equals the closure of s: closure (s ^ n) = closure s.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Combine the new closure_pow_le (giving closure (s^n) ≤ closure s for all n) with the existing lemma subset_pow (which gives the reverse inclusion closure s ≤ closure (s^n) under the hypotheses 1 ∈ s and n ≠ 0). The proof is a single antisymm application: closure_pow_le.antisymm (subset_pow hs hn).

pr_summary: Add an equality form for the difference of finset cardinalities: prove #t - #s = #(t \ s) - #(s \ t) and keep the existing inequality #t - #s ≤ #(t \ s) derived from it.

declarations.name: Finset.eq_card_diff_of_sdiff
declarations.nl_statement: For finsets s and t, the difference of their cardinalities equals the difference of the sizes of their relative complements: #t - #s = #(t \ s) - #(s \ t).
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Partition s into (s ∩ t) and (s \ t), so #s = #(s ∩ t) + #(s \ t). Substitute into #t - #s to get #t - #(s ∩ t) - #(s \ t). Use the identity #t - #(s ∩ t) = #(t \ (s ∩ t)) (card removing the intersection) and simplify t \ (s ∩ t) = t \ s to obtain #(t \ s) - #(s \ t). The Lean proof performs these algebraic/cardinality manipulations via the file's `grind` automation in three steps.
declarations.divergence: Very small: the proof follows the straightforward set-partition algebra; the Lean proof uses the `grind` tactic to carry out the routine rewriting steps.

declarations.name: Finset.le_card_sdiff
declarations.nl_statement: For finsets s and t, #t - #s ≤ #(t \ s).
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: This follows from eq_card_diff_of_sdiff by rewriting #t - #s as #(t \ s) - #(s \ t) and observing #(s \ t) ≥ 0, so subtracting it yields a number ≤ #(t \ s). The Lean proof simply invokes the `grind` automation to perform that calculation.
declarations.divergence: Negligible: direct consequence of the equality and nonnegativity of cardinalities; the proof is automated by `grind`.

pr_summary: Refactor and extend the API around rounding: add a formula for round in terms of Int.floor, simplify round proofs by using that formula, provide an alternative characterization round_eq_iff, and add topological continuity/tendsto facts for round and floor/ceil.

declarations.name: Mathlib.Algebra.Order.Round.round_eq'
declarations.nl_statement: For a LinearOrderedRing with floor structure, round x equals (⌊2*x⌋ + 1) / 2.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Rewrite 2*x as 2*(⌊x⌋ + fract x) using floor_add_fract. Expand definitions (fract_intCast_add, floor_intCast_add, ceil_intCast_add) and use integer-cast algebra lemmas (Int.mul_add_ediv_left) to put the RHS in the desired ediv form. Split on the if in the definition of round; in each branch use floor/ceil characterizations (floor_eq_iff / ceil_eq_iff) together with simple inequalities about fract (0 ≤ fract < 1) to show the two sides coincide.
declarations.divergence: The proof closely follows the algebraic manipulations one would do on paper; a few low-level lemma rewrites and case-splitting steps are present but directly reflect the intended argument.

declarations.name: Mathlib.Algebra.Order.Round.round_eq_half_ceil_two_mul
declarations.nl_statement: If 2*fract x ≠ 1, then round x = ⌈2*x⌉ / 2 (i.e. away from half-fraction points, rounding equals half the ceiling of 2x).
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Distinguish whether 2*x is an integer (case analysis on membership in range Int.cast). If 2*x is an integer, analyze parity of that integer: if even the formula reduces to the integer-case round, if odd this contradicts the hypothesis (2*fract x = 1) via two_mul_fract_eq_one_iff_exists_int. In the non-integer case use the previously proven round_eq' formula and the equivalence ceil = floor+1 when not an integer to convert the floor-based formula to a ceil-based one.
declarations.divergence: A direct case split reflecting the obvious mathematical cases (2x integral or not) with parity consideration; the proof is routine and mirrors the pen-and-paper reasoning.

declarations.name: Mathlib.Algebra.Order.Round.round_eq
declarations.nl_statement: Over a LinearOrderedField, round x = ⌊x + 1/2⌋.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Reduce to the ring-based formula round_eq' by casting and using the lemma cast_mul_floor_div_cancel_of_pos for 2 to move from (⌊2*x⌋ + 1)/2 to ⌊x+1/2⌋, then simplify the remaining algebraic terms (mul_add).
declarations.divergence: Very small: takes the previously established integer-floor formula and a straightforward algebraic identity to reach the classical characterization; the proof is compact and directly follows the standard algebraic manipulation.

declarations.name: Mathlib.Algebra.Order.Round.round_eq_iff
declarations.nl_statement: Over a LinearOrderedField, round x = n ↔ x ∈ Ico (n - 1/2) (n + 1/2).
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Unfold round via round_eq (⌊x+1/2⌋) and apply the usual floor characterization floor_eq_iff to translate equality of the floor into the double inequality that exactly describes membership in the closed-open interval Ico (n-1/2, n+1/2). Tidy the arithmetic with norm_num/rewrites to get the interval endpoints in the stated form.
declarations.divergence: None significant: a one-line equivalence that follows immediately from round_eq and the standard floor characterization.

declarations.name: Mathlib.Algebra.Order.Floor.Ring.ceil_intCast_add
declarations.nl_statement: For a FloorRing, ⌈z + a⌉ = z + ⌈a⌉ for z : ℤ, a : R (i.e., integer translation commutes with ceil).
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Reduce the statement to the already-proved lemma ceil_add_intCast by swapping the arguments using add_comm, both sides are equal up to commutativity of addition, then apply the existing lemma and commutativity again.
declarations.divergence: Trivial rewrite proof; it is essentially a one-line manipulation using add_comm and the existing ceil_add_intCast lemma.

declarations.name: Mathlib.Algebra.Order.Floor.Ring.ceil_natCast_add
declarations.nl_statement: For a FloorRing and n : ℕ, ⌈n + a⌉ = n + ⌈a⌉ (specializing integer translation for natural numbers).
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: This is a straightforward corollary of ceil_intCast_add by casting n : ℕ to ℤ and using mod_cast; the proof delegates to the integer version.
declarations.divergence: Directly follows from the integer case via casting; no conceptual divergence.

declarations.name: Mathlib.Algebra.Order.Floor.Ring.ceil_one_add
declarations.nl_statement: For a FloorRing, ⌈1 + a⌉ = 1 + ⌈a⌉.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Specialize ceil_natCast_add to n = 1 (mod_cast) and simplify; trivial by delegation to the nat-case.
declarations.divergence: None: immediate corollary of the nat-case.

declarations.name: Mathlib.Algebra.Order.Floor.Ring.ceil_ofNat_add
declarations.nl_statement: For a FloorRing and ofNat(n) with n ≥ 2, ⌈ofNat(n) + a⌉ = ofNat(n) + ⌈a⌉.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Obtain this by applying ceil_natCast_add to the natural number n and casting as needed; the proof is a direct mod_cast application to the general integer/nat lemma.
declarations.divergence: None significant: routine specialization and casting.

declarations.name: Mathlib.Topology.Algebra.Order.Floor.tendsto_round_nhdsGE_pure
declarations.nl_statement: Under the usual topological hypotheses, Tendsto round (𝓝[≥] x) (pure (round x)) — floor of round is eventually constant on right neighborhoods (round is eventually constant from the right at x).
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Use the algebraic round_eq' representation and the fact that the map n ↦ (n+1)/2 is an integer-to-integer map composed with floor of 2*·. Show that multiplying by 2 maps right neighborhoods to right neighborhoods (Tendsto (2*·) (𝓝[≥] x) (𝓝[≥] (2*x))). Then compose the known tendsto for integer floor on right neighborhoods (tendsto_floor_right_pure_floor applied to 2*x) with this scaling, and finally compose with the discrete map sending ⌊2*·⌋ to (⌊2*·⌋+1)/2 to get the pure tendency result.
declarations.divergence: The proof follows the standard filter-based topological argument; the chain of composed tendsto results is a bit more technical than the rough mathematical statement but faithful to it.

declarations.name: Mathlib.Topology.Algebra.Order.Floor.tendsto_round_nhdsLT_pure_half_ceil
declarations.nl_statement: Under the same hypotheses, Tendsto round (𝓝[<] x) (pure (⌈2*x⌉ / 2)) — from the left, round approaches the half-ceiling value of 2x.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Again use the round_eq' formula and the behavior of floor on left neighborhoods for 2*x: show Tendsto (2*·) (𝓝[<] x) (𝓝[<] (2*x)) and compose with the appropriate tendsto_floor_left_pure_ceil_sub_one statement for 2*x. Finally simplify to get the pure limit equal to ⌈2*x⌉/2 and use filter arithmetic to finish.
declarations.divergence: Similar to the previous tendsto entry: a routine but slightly technical composition of known tendsto facts; reads like a faithful formalization of the standard argument.

declarations.name: Mathlib.Topology.Algebra.Order.Floor.continuousAt_round
declarations.nl_statement: Under OrderClosedTopology and add-continuity and away from points where 2*fract x = 1, the function round is continuous at x.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Reduce continuity at x to left and right tendsto conditions. Use tendsto_round_nhdsLT_pure_half_ceil for the left neighborhood and tendsto_round_nhdsGE_pure for the right neighborhood. For the left-hand side, use the equality round = ⌈2*·⌉ / 2 away from the half-fraction points (round_eq_half_ceil_two_mul) to identify the correct pure limit. Use small filter-manipulation lemmas (pure_le_nhds_iff, mono_left/mono_right) and a final gcongr to tidy the inclusion of intervals. The proof is a direct assembly of the previously established tendsto facts to check the two-sided continuity criterion.
declarations.divergence: The argument mirrors the standard two-sided continuity proof via one-sided limits; the main complexity is bookkeeping of filters and using the earlier algebraic lemma to identify the left limit.

declarations.name: Mathlib.Topology.Algebra.Order.Floor.continuousOn_round
declarations.nl_statement: Under the same hypotheses, round is continuous on the set {x | 2*fract x ≠ 1} (i.e. continuous everywhere except the half-fraction points).
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: This is a direct corollary of continuousAt_round: given x in the domain where 2*fract x ≠ 1, apply continuousAt_round and convert pointwise continuity to continuity on the set via continuousWithinAt.
declarations.divergence: Direct and immediate from the pointwise continuity result; no divergence.
